JEPA has been something we follow very closely, and over the last couple of weeks, @ylecun and his collaborators at AMI Labs, NYU, and Brown have made huge progress with it. I reached out to @randall_balestr , who co-authored "Counterfactual World Models", to ask what he found most interesting in the paper. He told me that touch might be the frontier of what offline data can teach a robot. A video of a hand barely missing a mug doesn't tell you what would've happened if it had touched it. Maybe robots need to try things for themselves to learn. That conversation inspired me to make this video. I walk through two papers in detail (but keep it accessible): 1. The Content–Geometry Tradeoff in World Models: A JEPA can learn the layout of a city walk from first-person views and movement commands, without GPS! But in a separate experiment, it can lose track of a cube sitting right in front of it. The proposed fix, Slow SVReg, helps the model hold on to details that don’t change much from one frame to the next. 2. JEPAs that ask “What if?” (Counterfactual World Models) Say a current pushed your boat off course. Where would you have ended up if you’d steered left in that same current? With residual reuse, you take the gap between where you landed and where JEPA predicted you’d land, then add it to the prediction for steering left. Watch this video explainer to see the whole picture with demos, visuals, and Randall's full note to get a feel for it. Also, on Youtube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oaIgPi4OLcU Media

"If printing money would end poverty, printing diplomas would end stupidity." Javier Milei. This is France's problem in one sentence. We did with degrees what central banks do with money: we printed them until they were worth nothing. The master's degree has become a debased currency. And like all inflation, it leaves no visible victims. It quietly destroys the signal. The result: average people, holding some forgettable master's from a second-rate university, sincerely believe they belong to the elite. They have the title. They have the stamp. They expect the status that's supposed to come with it. And when reality refuses to hand it over, they conclude the system is unfair. But that's not even the real tragedy. The real tragedy is that when everyone has the same degree, the degree says nothing. Truly brilliant people become invisible, drowned in a sea of identical CVs. We built a machine that makes mediocrity comfortable and excellence undetectable. A country doesn't move forward because of how many graduates it produces. It moves forward because of a handful of exceptional people it knows how to spot, fund, and let build. France doesn't need more graduates. It needs more brilliant people, recognized as brilliant for what they built, not for the paper on their wall. Your degree says what you studied. What you built says who you are. Printing diplomas never created intelligence. Only inflation.
Our gift is about so much more than money. It’s about teaching an entire generation of young Americans the power of investing, compound interest and ownership. 🇺🇸🚀

I continue to be amazed by how well agent teams work. In other words, it's the idea of having a chief of staff, chief research officer, and other important agent roles. It has allowed me to scale work with agents, and it has also helped keep tasks organized as it scales. Roles, identities, and specialization will remain important primitives as we unlock collective intelligence in agents and scale with agent swarms. To be clear, I don't use any of the popular tools for this, like Grok Bot, Hermes, or personal agents. I have built my own solution, like with everything else. But I have been surprised by how great this all works, even though it's a simple implementation. Memory is key to making it all work because you need to persist important knowledge and preferences. Clearly define the agents' roles in the team. Set up clear permissions as well. But you also need good solutions for coordination and automation. Use a minimal solution to ingest and track events and schedules. Let me know if you have any questions. I am happy to share more details on any of these.

Must-read paper on recursive collective intelligence. Highly recommend if you are planning to use agent swarms. They find that an agent team beats AIs working alone only when each one knows something the others don't and shares it. This aligns with my suspicion that collective intelligence comes from pooling different knowledge. Adding more AIs that all know the same things doesn't make the group smarter. This is particularly important if you are trying to build agent swarms. This work specifically asks if agent teams can improve recursively at the same compute budget. They check whether that gain comes from teamwork or from extra compute. A team uses many more tokens than one agent. Running several agents on their own with the same token budget and taking a majority vote already explains most of the gain. So the authors test each team against three bars, all at the same compute. The team has to beat one agent. Then it has to beat a majority vote of independent agents. The hardest bar is a group of independent agents where a task counts as solved if any one of them gets it right. Teamwork cleared the hardest bar only when each agent held different facts and passed them on to the others. In that setup, teams beat the hardest bar at three model sizes, by about a third with 27B models. Teams of identical 27B agents also organized themselves without being told to. A few agents became hubs that collected and shared information, and accuracy rose 18 points. Groups then trained their next generation on their own verified outputs, with no labels. On PlanBench, HiddenBench, and Hanabi, each generation beat the previous one on unseen problems for four to six generations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32606 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/recursive-collective-intelligence-emergence-on-an-equal-budget-ladder-in-multi-a-2611.32606

New paper from Microsoft and colleagues on personalized agent harnesses. If you build personalized assistants on top of user memory, this one is worth your time. The harness for a personalized agent is the memory and control code that connects a user's history to its answers. One shared workflow for all users is cheap but cannot adapt. Optimizing a separate harness per user adapts, but it needs a scored search for every user. HyperHarness trains one generator across many users. Given a user's history, a construction LLM writes retrieval and answer-guidance functions for that user. Task scores across training users refine the generator, and the answering model is never updated. At deployment, the frozen generator builds a harness for a new user in one pass. Across PersonaMemv3, Mem-PAL, and MemoryCD with three answering models, it had the best aggregate score in seven of nine settings and beat the strongest baselines by up to 5.95 points. It used 90.32% fewer answer-time tokens than long-context prompting. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29062 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/hyperharness-learning-to-generate-personalized-agent-harnesses-from-user-histori-2611.29062
